utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, take a chair. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, this morning assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with John Ackerman. We're assisted by Aleksandar Vujic today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. And thank you. Any preliminaries? You have been informed by Mr. Roberts about the tomorrow's meeting? Not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I may have. I haven't read any emails that I may have received over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Because I gave the go-ahead so you should have received a communication. If you haven't, please let me know after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tomorrow morning, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, tomorrow morning at 11.00, if I remember well. Or it could be 11.30, Mr. Ackerman. Okay? Thank you. As there are no other preliminaries, could I ask the usher to escort Mr. Neskovic in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome once more. We are going to proceed with your testimony here, and you are testifying on the basis of the same solemn declaration that you made last Friday which need not be repeated today. So please take a chair, and Ms. Korner will proceed with her series of questions. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something before the Prosecutor takes the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Prosecutor. I wanted to say that last time in my testimony there was a mistake that was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- I did. I said on the 16th of July 1992 that the detention against three individuals was revoked and that the rest were transferred to Banja Luka and then to Doboj. However, when I looked at my letter of the 17th of July, I saw that one individual remained in Teslic in hospital there. So it wasn't 13 individuals, it was a matter of 12 individuals, in actual fact. And may I add something else, please, with the Court's indulgence. You asked me whether I had released the detainee inside Banja Luka, and my answer was that I did not. And that Jovo Rosic didn't either. When I leafed through the interview that the investigating judge, Kovacevic, gave to the papers, I came across a sentence there which I would like to read out. And it is interesting with respect to the release from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has got a newspaper article part of which we've had translated. But it's an interview with the judge, Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Neskovic, please go ahead. And read slowly, please, because the interpreters probably don't have a copy of what you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Kovacevic says, and I quote, "The detainees in the district prison of Doboj were transferred in the second half of 1993." I think this is a journalist error, this 1993 bit. "It is interesting to note that only certain individuals" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please, sir. Your Honour, he is, in fact, reading from the part we've had translated so we may as well hand them out now, so that Your Honours can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Let's go through this again. In the meantime, usher.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the document be placed on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy, Ms. Korner? If you have an extra copy perhaps in English we could have it placed on the ELMO for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, that will become 2732.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please start all over again. Start reading the part you were reading before. Could you start again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The detainees were transferred to the Doboj district prison in the second half of 1993. The interesting thing is that only some people were taken to the Doboj prison then, while the others were transferred only when I, as the court president, informed the then-prison warden Bosko Djukic that all detainees must, according to the ruling of the court, be transferred to the Doboj prison." And I conclude from that that Kovacevic did have some contacts with the warden, and I came to understand that the prisoners should have been in Doboj. Now, this last sentence, "they must be transferred to the prison in Doboj," that's what I'm referring to, that all detainees "must" be transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose while we are at this I might as well ask you to read the whole paragraph. Could you please start from a few lines up where Kovacevic starts with the words: "A very strange situation occurs..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you start from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Kovacevic says: "A very strange situation occurs. Without the knowledge of the district judge, who is the only one authorised to make decisions about the detention and the treatment of the detainees, they are transferred from the Tunjice district prison to the district prison of Doboj. I learnt about it from ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pause, pause, pause, pause. Which district judge is he referring to here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not clear to anybody. He's the judge that's supposed to decide on their fate. And I didn't understand who the district judge was because the district judges were not the competent people to deal with first-instance cases, but only to deal with appeals. And, Your Honour, this says "pursuant to the ruling of the regular court the 20th of May 1992." The basic courts were really competent for the first-instance cases where all crimes are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Continue reading, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In order to establish what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened, I went to the district court of Banja Luka and asked the court president, Jovo Rosic, to tell me what happened. He was not able to respond to my question, but he gave me a fax he received from the then-Doboj high court president Goran Neskovic who demanded that these people be transferred. The detainees were transferred to the district prison in the second half of 1993. The interesting thing is that only some people were taken to the Doboj district prison then, while the others were transferred only when I, as the court president, informed the then-prison warden Bosko Djukic by sending him a general letter that all detainees must according to the ruling of the court be transferred to the Doboj prison." So I'm not at all clear that they were transferred on two occasions, as I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it strike you as odd or exceptional that Judge Neskovic thought it was necessary for him to travel to Banja Luka and query this up -- Judge Kovacevic thought it best to travel to Banja Luka in those circumstances and thrash this matter out with the judge -- court president Jovo Rosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovo Rosic wasn't the person that should have been in charge of that case. And he had nothing to deliberate in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm saying to you, what would have prompted -- what would have prompted Judge Kovacevic to take the trouble to go to Banja Luka and thrash this matter out with Judge Rosic, President Rosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably he had been informed and had received my fax. I assume he had received my fax. Jovo Rosic, that is, and that he was informed about that fax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you sure that you had informed Judge Kovacevic that you had sent this fax to President Rosic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence was that he didn't inform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't. I didn't inform him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Judge Kovacevic could only hear about what was happening from the papers, from the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that the media could have published that if on the 17th the fax left, that was a Friday, when the fax was sent out, the 18th was a Saturday. The 19th, and then the 20th they were transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we will come to this later. I have got some further questions on exactly what happened and the big tug of war that there was at the time on this matter in particular between Doboj and Teslic. We'll come to that later, Mr. Neskovic. Yes, Ms. Korner, do you have any further statements that you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just wanted to add one thing, the Prosecutor asked me whether it was because of the release of these prisoners I became a member of the crisis staff, and so was promoted in that way. I said I wasn't a member of that crisis staff. But however, when I looked through my documents, that a crisis staff didn't even exist. It was the war presidency that existed. The crisis staff had been abolished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and were you a member of the war presidency at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It was strictly prescribed in the law who could be a member of the war presidencies, and that could have been the president of the municipality or his deputy, or rather the vice-president of the executive council and his deputy, and the vice-president or one of the deputies, citizens' deputies, and that is a decision of the 31st of May 1992, and it was published on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're confirming that you never were a member of either a crisis staff or a war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While Jovo Rosic, who was also president of the Banja Luka high court, was indeed a member of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these rules did not seem to apply to him, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in the regulations of Republika Srpska. There were no regulations linked to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It was an internal district, just for Krajina, whereas Doboj did not belong to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I anticipate Ms. Korner has a lot of questions in the pipeline for you. So Ms. Korner, I'm so sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Questioned by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just make it clear to you that I wasn't suggesting that you became a member of the crisis staff or the war presidency as a result of releasing these men, but I was asking whether you had in May become a member of the crisis staff, and you said that was an error by a witness. I want to go back over one matter that you were asked about no less than three, if not four times by the Judges last week. And you were asked by Judge Agius at page 22 of the LiveNote: "who had ordered their transfer to Banja Luka?" That is the Mice prisoners. And your reply was: "The president said only the police from Banja Luka. That was the only information I had. The police from Banja Luka." And then Judge Agius asked you again: "It seems that these detainees were transferred. Were they transferred by the judge or were they just transferred by the security services or by the police, or the military to Banja Luka?" Your answer, again: "I don't think the judge did that." And you said on two further occasions that as you understood it, it was the police of their own initiative who had transferred those people to Banja Luka. Now, you know that's absolutely incorrect, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you who transferred them and whether it was the judge. I wasn't in Teslic. But I assume that the police conducts the transfer of prisoners. Now, whether the judge gave the order for that or not, I cannot say because I wasn't informed. He just said that the police had transferred the prisoners to Banja Luka. And I'm referring to the transfer. Now what the agreement was between Kovacevic and the police and the rest of them, the prosecutors, I really don't know because I wasn't present so I can't say. I can't tell you something I don't know about because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the physical transfer was done by the police, but in the end you accepted they could not have been transferred without an order from the judge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes. The judge must issue an order determining detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that no one outside the investigating judge who was empowered to deal with these alleged crimes could release prisoners from custody, save for an appeal to your court?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to come back to the last thing you told us on Friday afternoon when we looked at those documents, a series of forms authorising release.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've forgotten the number, I'm afraid, Your Honour, but it must be 2731, I think. Perhaps the witness could have them back. We'll have the translation on the ELMO, please. There's a translation there, one page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is what you said about this. You acknowledged that these were your signatures, and you said: "Last week in the archives of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the district court I took out this letter" - that's the fax - "and together -- and along with it were these statements which I brought as evidence that they were in prison. When they were transferred to the prison, someone informed me that they were asking to take a bath. I asked each of them for a guarantee that after taking a bath, they would immediately return to the prison, that they should sign this. And when they brought this, I signed it and put it in the archives as evidence that they had reported to the prison and that if they didn't they should have detention ordered." Do you still stand by that answer you gave on the last thing on Friday, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but we didn't complete it because we interrupted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What else would you like to say about this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: I didn't compile these statements. They were compiled by the prison administration because if I was asking a court to transfer prisoners from a prison, I also would ask for guarantees that they would be transferred, that they wouldn't escape, and once they had had their bath they would be back in prison because otherwise I would bear the responsibility because I made the request and the case was a complex one. So for that reason, I asked that each of them individually -- I asked the prison administration that each of them sign a statement like this when they were taken over so that I could have those statements in the court because should anybody escape or not return, that a warrant could be put out for his apprehension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, you agree that between the 18th and 21st of July all of these men were in custody, either in Banja Luka prison or Doboj. Nobody had released them; no order had been made for their release.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, did you say the 24th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 21st of July when the public prosecutor agreed to the release of the military people back to the military.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise. May I be allowed to clarify. Something has not been made quite clear. The investigating judge on the 21st of July made the ruling, and it didn't reach the prison on the 21st of July because the post wasn't working. There wasn't a courier service. The actual document arrived on the 24th July, and they were released at 15.10 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you misunderstood. The release of these men was ordered by Judge Kovacevic on the 21st of July, and they may not have been released until the 24th.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But between the 18th of July when you sent the telex asking for the transfer to Doboj prison and until the judge made the order, all of those people were lawfully in custody?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What power did you have to say that these men should be released to take a bath?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No power except humaneness because they hadn't taken a bath for a month, and they were in detention anyway. So a bath after a month, and as you could see the statements were signed in Banja Luka, so it was only that day. When they came, they had a bath and were in detention. The statements were signed on the 18th of July when they were in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you on the 18th of July, which is when you signed these documents, that these men wanted a bath?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't sign it on the 18th of July. The statements were their signatures were brought to me, and then on the 20th I certified them with my signature and archived them. As you can see, this is their handwriting. Everyone filled in these statements, signed them, and dated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at the date below your signature on each of those documents.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of July. In the case of Kezunovic, for Sljivic, there's no date, et cetera. There's one corrected date, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you sign these release documents on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just telling you, they signed them on the 18th of July. And these statements were brought to me. And then I certified them with my signature and archived them. It is no evidence if it says the 18th of July that the detainees signed it because there's no date below my signature. If I had put on such-and-such a date the president of the court and then my signature, then we would know the exact date when I signed it. I agree with you that there's no authority for me to release them to have a bath because the 17th was a Friday, the 18th a Saturday, the 19th a Sunday, and Monday was the 20th. So it was a weekend, there was no communication with anyone, with the investigating judge of anyone. So the only reason were reasons of humaneness, and I admit that. And if I have to bear responsibility for this, I will. But I think for someone not to have a bath for a month is also not permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. This deviation regarding the date actually led to his not answering the question that you had put to him, which is actually who had informed him that these men wanted a bath.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. You're right. I would have been taken down the deviation as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that these men wanted a bath?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these statements are forms, printed forms. And they were taken to Banja Luka. It's not just having a bath; it is for security for them that they will reach Doboj from Banja Luka. When they come to Doboj, they have a bath and after that they go to prison. So his statement is that from Banja Luka he will report to prison. No one is escorting them. They went alone with the driver, and this is a guarantee that once released in Banja Luka they would reach Doboj. That is what I keep repeating, linked to the bath and to transport. Those statements were signed in Banja Luka. And they were brought to me, I initialled them and kept them as guarantee that they reached prison, that they hadn't escaped. If they had escaped, I would have issued a warrant for their arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can we go back to the question, please. Your original answer was you were told by the prison that these men wanted a bath. Who told you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you from the prison?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember now. Perhaps one should ask who was the organiser in the prison itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you having direct contact with the prison when, as you told us on Friday, you had no authority to get these men transferred, you had to make the request to Rosic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I did make the request to Rosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why were you having any kind of direct contact with the prison?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was afraid because of the fax I had sent to Rosic that once those men leave Banja Luka they might escape. I took upon myself a high degree of responsibility for them in doing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a degree of responsibility which was totally outside the law. That's right, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite outside the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it within the law?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our laws, there are certain possibilities when the accused may give a statement that they will respond to a call-up from the prison or the authorities, and this was done for reasons of humaneness and for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just look at the picture, shall we. You send a fax, a request, because you have no power, to Jovo Rosic to transfer these men from Banja Luka prison to Doboj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time you receive some kind of communication that these men want a bath, and you draw up release forms which are beyond your competence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. When those men went to Banja Luka, they took these statements with them for security reasons. For each of them to sign that they will come to Doboj from Banja Luka, that they would not escape, that they could have a bath during the weekend, and that they would go to prison. It's not just a link to the bath, it's the entire procedure, from Banja Luka to Doboj, because I fear that they could jump off the bus and escape. So that would mean that I had asked for their transfer, and then they escaped. What I wanted was to provide security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But can you answer the question, please, sir. This form should either have been signed by Rosic or by Kovacevic, but not by you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did so because I was afraid of the consequences as I had made the request. And that is why I brought this document to show them to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but as you say, sir, it was a request which could have been refused by Rosic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was Rosic who would be responsible for the release, not you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would have to be held responsible if I was the one who asked them to be transferred to Doboj and the prison administration in Doboj would say that I was responsible. Rosic would say I handed them over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these people who had been arrested for killings, looting, robbery were transferred in a bus without any security save a driver?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that that was my assumption because the police were engaged on the front. That was my assumption. I wasn't with them. Nowadays, that would not happen. There's security, vans, police vans, and everything. These were old buses that the men would board and go with a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, that is what you assumed would happen, that there would be no police escort, but you were prepared to take that risk rather than leave them in Banja Luka prison where they could be investigated by Mr. Peric and Judge Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had all been investigated, or rather interrogated. Kovacevic came to Doboj to interrogate them, and all other cases. All his detainees from Teslic were in Doboj as far as I know. There wasn't a single case in Banja Luka from Teslic. All the other cases of persons held in custody were there, were dealt with there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the reason, I suggest, which was explained to you why Judge Kovacevic had ordered these men to be detained in Banja Luka was because of the situation that existed between the police in Doboj and the police in Teslic, and he did not think that it was safe for them to be kept in Doboj. He explained that to you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason that these men were free walking the streets of Doboj on the 20th of July as reported in that newspaper was entirely due to your illegal granting of what I will call provisional release for them to go and have a bath?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that there was anything in the media. I just know that the investigating judge and the prosecutor visit them in detention, and that they dropped in to see me while they were in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The article was read to you on Friday where the complaint was that these men were seen on the 20th of July on the streets of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard and read about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, you read it yourself last Friday. Do you want to have another look at it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't need to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only reason that those men were on the street seen by the general public was because you had granted this order for release. That's right, isn't it? Otherwise, they would have been in Doboj prison.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, first of all, I don't know what public you're referring to when you're saying they were in Doboj. There was no public in Doboj because people were in their basements every day because of the shelling. Secondly, when they brought these statements to me, I hadn't seen the detainees in the streets, nor in prison, nor did I have any contact with them. And the investigating judge saw for himself where they were because he visited them. So he could have denied that this was not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, the suggestion to you is that this was public knowledge, and I think -- I can also put it to you that there was no one in Teslic and no one in Doboj who was not completely aware that these men were out in the streets in Doboj on the 20th of July, and that you are going around in circles here to avoid telling us the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look again, please, at 1938, P-1-9-3-8, the report. Turn to paragraph 10, please. On the 20th of July 1992, the public prosecutor and the investigating judge learned from the chief of the Teslic SJB crime investigation service that all the accused had been released from the Banja Luka district prison and that they were free. And the only reason they were free was as a result of your order which was an illegal one, wasn't it? You had no power to issue it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite contrary to the interview given by Judge Kovacevic because you see, the investigating judge has learned that all the accused have been released from the prison in Banja Luka and that they were free, whereas in the interview he says that he went there and gave general instructions for all of them to be released. So I think that this report is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, stop. This is a report sent to the government of the Serbian Republic by the Office of the Public Prosecutor. Now, what he says in the interview that he gave is that only some people were taken to the Doboj prison. But never mind that. This is what the report says. Now, do you agree if they were free on the 20th of July, it was because of this order that you gave? Sir, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Do I agree that...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only way that these men could have been on the street, and I'll come on to the next bit in a moment, on the 20th of July is because you had issued this order granting them release?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might accept it if somebody saw them on the 20th of July when they were going to prison. But this report is not correct because it says here that they have to report on the 20th of July. As far as I know, they reached Doboj on the 20th of July. They did come to Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they were let out of the prison van to wander the streets to go and have a bath. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To have a bath and to return to prison, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so unless everybody in the streets of Doboj was hiding in a bunker somewhere, the public could have seen them wandering the streets to get a bath?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't see them on the 21st and the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at the end of that paragraph, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 10?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It has been learned informally that the arrival was celebrated outside the CSB building and that they were all released." I'm not aware of this and it is not true. Nothing was celebrated of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have heard of it. I think it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move to what you had to say about all this --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. As far as I can see, this is a text taken from the newspaper Glas of the 24th of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is three or four days later obviously. So if they celebrated on the 20th and were released, then it should have been reported on the 21st, 22nd, 23rd. Why on the 24th? On the 24th, these others were released. But I'm not aware of any of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to have a look, please, at what you yourself said when you gave an interview to Nezavisne Novine on the 13th of October 1999, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, we've got copies. Your Honour, this will become a new exhibit. It's 2733.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that Nezavisne Novine had run a series of articles on notorious war crimes during 1999. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The editor of the newspaper being a journalist called Zeljko Kopanja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nezavisne Novine, yes, I think he's the owner of this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Owner and editor. This was dated the 13th October --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and we'll look at the lead article in the paper in a moment. And on the 22nd of October, a bomb was placed under his car, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that that was so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his legs were blown off?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that. I'm a friend of the journalist's, and I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nobody has ever been arrested or prosecuted for that, have they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm an attorney. I wasn't working in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. But you are an attorney working, what? Still in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would have heard, wouldn't you, if there had been any arrest or prosecution for a crime as grave as that one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this was on the 13th of October 1999. At the time, I was living in Belgrade, and it was only in the year 2000 that I returned to Doboj. I had a registered office in Doboj, but I was working in Belgrade. But I heard about all this, and I read about it in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we look, please, at some of the things that you said in answer to the journalist's questions. It was put to you that you insisted that the Mice be transferred to Doboj prison of which there is evidence in the form of a fax that you sent to the president of the Banja Luka high court. And you gave to the journalist the same explanation that you had given us and stated that the transfer of the prisoners to Banja Luka prison was illegal. And you rely for that, do you, illegality on some regulations which you don't have with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have them with me. I read them out. It's the organisation -- it's a decision on the organisation of courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We went through that last time. That says that Teslic comes under the Doboj high court. It says nothing about the fact that anybody arrested has to be kept in Doboj prison as opposed to anywhere else. Does it, sir? We went through that yesterday -- on Friday.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you go, please, to the end of the answer you gave - this is on page 3 of the translation - to the question: "It's well known that Teslic was caught in the regional dispute between Banja Luka and Doboj" et cetera. The last sentence of that answer, or last two sentences: "The decision to release them from detention was signed by the investigating judge in Teslic and it should still be in the Doboj prison archives. So it wasn't me who released the Mice from detention, it couldn't have been me in the first place because the proceedings were conducted by the Teslic basic court, and they were the ones who decided to let them go. I only asked that they be transferred to the Doboj prison, and I didn't get involved in the case any further." That was not true, was it, sir, as we have just seen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What is it that I said in my testimony today? I also said that the investigating judge took all the decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but we have just been for the last 20 minutes or so, sir, going through the reason -- just listen. Going through the reasons why you gave authority for these men to be released. Why didn't you tell the newspaper that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when I was giving this interview I had no documents with me. And it was given because I was criticised in a previous issue for cooperating with the international prosecutor because those people believed that I had activated the case in the media, which was not true. And if you check that out, you will see that I was criticised. When I was giving this interview, I had no documents on me. It was only last week when I came to the Tribunal that I found the documents and prepared them. At the time, I was speaking on the basis of my recollections, which may not be correct. And this was an interview for the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go on, one of the many oddities about this case, sir, is this, isn't it, that the court file has gone missing? That's right, isn't it, sir? Because that's one of the things that comes up in these articles.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you have the file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's what you said to the investigators, to the newspaper, that you're perfectly well aware, aren't you, that since 1993 the actual court file has been missing. Bits of documents are available, but not the court file. You know that, sir, don't you? Because it's one of the things that's raised.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What year are you referring to? 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest in 1993 you took over the court file.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe you are mistaken. Do you mean 1996? I think that's an error on your part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may well be right, sir. But in any event, you were the last person -- that's right. I'm so sorry. You're absolutely right, sir, and I take that back. 1996, the file was given to you. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to that file?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are now talking about 1996, we are discussing my role as a liaison officer, my role that I had in relations with you. If I need to talk about that, then I need to have protection pursuant to Rule 79, and I think that the hearing should be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to pursue this question and answer in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've heard the witness make the request. It's a matter for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Cunningham, do you have any remarks on this witness's specific request?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. So the position as it emerges, Mr. Neskovic, at a certain point in time in reply to a question put to you by Ms. Korner, at a certain point in time you acknowledge having received a request from MUP to hand over this file, and you effectively handed over this file, and you have in your possession a receipt to that effect which you have shown us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. I handed over that file, and I have a receipt for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your next question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's backtrack a little, shall we. This was the court file from the Teslic investigation which was still open four years after the event. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That court file was in Teslic. Why was it given to you? I'm sorry, why were you asked to hand it over to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had it. It was in the Ministry of Justice in actual fact. And I was the liaison officer, and I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why wasn't the file still in Teslic court?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he came to see me. Or rather, it came to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At your request?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that before or after the MUP had asked you to hand it over?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before. The file had reached me earlier on, two months prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that? Why had you taken over the file?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that question in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why didn't you, when the police asked for the file, decline to give it to them because they had no right to the court file, did they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that, as I say, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered that question, no. It's still -- private session or not private session, it's still a mystery why an ex-judge in particular, someone who knows exactly how the separation of jurisdiction should be between the executive and the judiciary, and who at a certain point in time happens to come back in possession of this court file, agrees to hand a court file to the police, out of all people, or to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that's what they asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why didn't you refuse? This is the question that was put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to interfere much, even though he is a court witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you just give a copy of the file? Why didn't you yourself just take a copy of the Teslic file and return it to the court so that they can continue with their investigations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought they would give it back after conducting the investigation, and I was informed that the file was at the MUP and that it was sent in 2001. I have been looking for it since 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When you -- for the purposes which you told us about you received the court file, why didn't you simply take a photocopy and then immediately, whatever purpose you received it for, return it to the Teslic court because they couldn't operate, they could do nothing without that file, and you knew that, didn't you, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that, but they didn't ask for it anymore. I informed them that I had given the file to the MUP, and they could have asked the MUP for it at any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us you took possession of this file for two reasons, one of which you told us about in private session. When you took possession of that file for the reason you told us about in private session, why didn't you just photocopy it and then return it immediately?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I didn't. I relied on the letter. What was important for me was to have a receipt that they had taken it over, and I didn't realise that the file would disappear. You can't have a file disappear. You can reconstruct any file. And it has already been reconstructed, in fact, on the basis of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move on to what was said on the same day in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going through the rest of this interview. It's there for anyone to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because there was a leading article published. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to hand them out. An editorial, I should say. Your Honour, can that be made, please, 2734.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to deal with some of the things that it says. Now, on -- in page 2 in the translation, can you find the paragraph that begins: "The reactions of certain participants in the events have led the story in a completely logical direction and opened up many dilemmas and issues. Naturally, one of them is who ordered the disappearance of the Teslic basic court criminal file containing the key evidence collected during the investigation which proves the criminal activities of the group which carried out the shocking campaign of terror. Explanations provided by lawyer Goran Neskovic who took the file in Teslic on behalf of the Ministry of Justice and then, according to his own words, handed it over to the Ministry of the Interior, constitute a poor and quite naive defence for a man who works in the field of law; namely, legal experts say that it is, in the best of cases, unusual for incomplete case files to be delivered to the Ministry of Justice, let alone the police. If, in the course of a court case, there are indications that another crime had been committed, it would be logical for the prosecutor or the judge to inform the police of it and request that appropriate actions be taken." Now, do you agree with the editorial that it is "unusual for incomplete case files to be delivered to the Ministry of Justice, let alone the police"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything's unusual. All of it. It's unusual that I worked as a liaison officer, too. Because I took all the court files, and that was changed by Dayton. I completely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I should have asked you this earlier. Did you ever ask the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP, for the return of that file?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the chance of doing that. The file was handed over in 1996. And after that, quite simply I did not communicate with them any more about the subject. And in 1997, the changes occurred. And it was only in 1999 when the article was published that I started collecting data and information and searching for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one of the things that you told us on Friday in response --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just be allowed to add: Nor did anybody contact me or ask me about the file. Nobody did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But whether they contacted you or not, sir, you were responsible for the removal of a court file which was an illegal act. Didn't you try and make efforts to get it returned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I informed the court that the file was with the MUP, so the court could contact the MUP directly. They didn't have to go through me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nonetheless, you were the person responsible in the same way as you have explained to us that you were responsible for the prisoners' move from Banja Luka to Doboj, why didn't you yourself make efforts to get it back?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered that I had completed my job by informing the court that the MUP had the file. I didn't undertake anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Theoretically, of course, you could have been prosecuted for that, couldn't you, the removal of the file?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I had handed it over at the request of MUP, and also because there is the letter saying that I handed it over personally. Then, in theory the president of the court must be held -- would have to be held responsible as well, who sent it to me. And had I not had this receipt, then in theory I could be held responsible for abusing my position and post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. One of the things you were asked about last week, last Friday by Judge Agius was this: "Do you know Mr. Brdjanin?" And you said you didn't know him in 1992. "I got to know him in 1994 or 1995, Mr. Trbojevic introduced us." And the Judge asked you to confirm this was Milan Trbojevic. And he asked you: "Was he minister of justice at one time in Republika Srpska?" "I don't think so," you said. "I think he was never the minister of justice." Go back, please, to this editorial.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant the question was for the minister of justice during the war. Mr. Trbojevic was justice minister only after the war, 1999 and 2000 for a brief period. I thought the question meant during the war. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Because we can see and you can see, can't you, from this editorial, that it is absolutely clear that he is the minister of justice? You can see, can't you? This article in the next paragraph says: "Today the mysterious disappearance of the court file is like a stone hanging around the necks of both minister Novic and the minister of justice Milan Trbojevic."

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was 1999 when the papers wrote about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said he was never minister of justice, you just meant during the war, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I meant it was a case from the war. I didn't know we would be discussing 1999 at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go finally please to the last paragraph -- not quite the last, but nearly the end of this editorial. "In 1992" - do you see that part? - "some 50 people were involved in these court proceedings, some as suspects, some as victims. They all have the right to know the truth, just as all those who were in one way or another singled out or maybe suspected of having taken part have that right. When we asked the former prosecutor, Branko Peric, what should now be done in this case, he told us to read what he proposed in 1992 in his request for investigation. It says there that Andrija Bjelosevic, chief of the Doboj CSB, his deputy Milan Savic, and the Doboj zone of operations chief of security should be interviewed as witnesses about the tasks of the accused Mice in Teslic and their authorisation." Were you aware of that, that was the recommendation that was made?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I'm just reading that request now, looking through it. And in the request to conduct an investigation, it says that it is proposed to the investigating judge to hear Andrija Bjelosevic, chief of the security service centre, and Milan Savic, deputy of the CSB, and the chief of security of the Doboj zone of operations should be interviewed within the frameworks of their authorisation. That's what the request says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know if you were aware of that at the time that you arranged for the transfer to Doboj of these imprisoned men.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have the file at my disposal. Kovacevic had the file, and I didn't know about a single document at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you discussed matters with Judge Kovacevic, did he explain to you that that was one of the proposed causes of action that was going to be taken by Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Peric didn't take steps at all. Mr. Peric just tabled a request to the judge for these hearings, but the judge didn't present anything. I didn't know about this, you can ask him, until I had the documents. So it's an investigation conducted by the judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the problem was, wasn't it, that any proper investigation might have shown that these men had been sent by the authorities, Mr. Bjelosevic, together with Mr. Perisic, into Teslic to chase up the disarmament programme? That was the problem, wasn't it, Mr. Neskovic? The involvement of the authorities in Republika Srpska might have been revealed if this had gone on. That's right, isn't it, sir? And you knew that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking here. What armaments programme?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you whether or not you at the time that you arranged for these men to be released, as I suggest you did, sir, did so on instructions from authorities.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. None of the authorities contacted me, and you can talk to them. It was my own initiative, and Kovacevic knows that. When I asked Jovo Rosic to be transferred to Doboj, just to abide by legal procedure, and you can talk to any witnesses you like. I was the only person to decide that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you took that series of actions from the 17th of July, which resulted in the transfer, the appearance on the streets of these arrested criminals entirely on your own initiative. That is what you are saying, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to say that I had asked Mr. Rosic to stick to legal procedure, and for the high court to remain the competent authority for the Teslic area. And as you can see from the interview, this is something Mr. Kovacevic agreed to at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, how much time do you require, and you will have as much time as you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm not going to use much time. I think if we could take the break now, I probably wouldn't use more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I would imagine so. We'll have a break of 25 minutes. And we'll take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neskovic. You are now going to be asked a series of questions by Mr. Cunningham who is co-counsel together with Mr. Ackerman defending Mr. Brdjanin in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham. Questioned by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to start off by showing you a portion of DB164. There's the copy in B/C/S, here's an English copy for the ELMO. What I'd like you to do when you get the B/C/S version is look at Article 28. The page that I'm showing you is from the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska dated 23 March 1992. The portion that we're dealing with is the law of internal affairs. So if you could look at Article 28 because what I think it does is it deals with the establishment of social -- excuse me, of offices of the Security Services Centre. I see you looking through some of your other documents. I want to make sure you're ready to answer. Let me know when you're ready. If we look at the B/C/S version of Article 28 it says, does it not, that there is a Security Services Centre to be established in Doboj for the Serb Autonomous Region of Northern Bosnia. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite correct. This is regulated by Article 28 of the law, and there was always a similar organisation for security services centres, a similar organisation applied to higher courts. To explain myself, when you have a security services centre, it covers certain municipalities, and the same municipalities are covered by higher courts. And that was the organisation before the war, during the war, and after the war. It says here is a security service centre is being established in Doboj for the Serbian Autonomous Region of Northern Bosnia, also in the law of the organisation of courts it is stipulated that a higher court is established to the Autonomous Region of Northern Bosnia. I looked through the -- some documents of mine, and I found a decision on the proclamation of the Serbian Autonomous Region in Bosnia-Herzegovina which indicates which towns should be included in the Autonomous Region of Northern Bosnia. That is Official Gazette number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my guess is if we were to consult that Official Gazette that you just referred to, we would see that the Municipality of Teslic fell under the jurisdiction of the Doboj CSB and the Doboj courts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbian Autonomous Region of Northern Bosnia, based in Doboj consisting of parts of municipalities with a majority Serb population, Teslic, Doboj, Tesanj, Derventa, Bosanski Brod, Odzak, Bosanski Samac, Modrica, Gradacac, Banovci, Zavidovici, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the English version, and I'm not asking you to do this, but we'll see there is a translation error because that portion of Article 28, talking about the establishment of a CSB in Doboj didn't get translated. But you've just confirmed that that was indeed the case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last Friday at page -- before we get to that, the head of the CSB in Doboj was Andrija Bjelosevic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was the individual that you characterised as having the most power in Doboj during 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I characterised him as the chief of police for the whole region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Page 21, last Friday, you said the following: "Up to the moment of the arrest" - we're talking about the Mice obviously - "as far as I know Teslic was under the control of the Doboj police, the Security Services Centre there. After the arrest, Teslic was controlled by the Banja Luka Security Services Centre. That's how it remain throughout the war. Now, again, it is under the control of the Doboj Security Services Centre." That document that is in front of you, the one that we referred to, DB164, confirms what you told the court last week about under which jurisdiction Doboj and Teslic -- under whose jurisdiction Doboj and Teslic was under the CSB. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I told Your Honours I'd be brief. And I'm done with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Janu. We have some final questions to put to you, sir. Judge Janu is going to start. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I have just a few simple questions for you, Mr. Neskovic. You said -- you told us that you left the judiciary in 1998. Can you give me the reason why you left the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, that is, in February of 1998, well-known changes occurred in the government. I was offered to remain in the ministry, but the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time officially appointed me liaison officer of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the International Tribunal. I held that position for a month or two. As they were unable to provide the necessary conditions, no salary or accommodation or offices, I requested that I be relieved of that duty and to be admitted to the bar as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So you answered my second question because I wanted to know who appointed you to the position to be a liaison officer. You said when you received the file concerning the Mice, you had this file for two months. Can you tell me why you kept the file so long? What you have done with the file? Maybe you needed it for something, so if you can assist the Chamber and give us the explanation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this file was handed over at the end of May or maybe beginning the June. I can't be precise about that. So it was there in June for the reasons I gave you in private session. And it was in June that representatives of Republika Srpska came to this Tribunal for the first time. So we were busy preparing documents and preparing our visit here. And then August came, and the request for the file. So as far as I can remember, that was the sequence of events during those summer months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So you haven't done anything concrete with the file? It was just with you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the writing office of the ministry waiting to be dispatched after I had copied it. And it was registered under a number in the records. It has a number. When we look for something, then we look for it in the protocol under a certain number, and it is registered in that protocol. Also, when the file went to the MUP, the number remained indicating that it was send out on such and such a date, and there's a signature. And if Your Honour's interested, I can read out from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: No, I am not after what you are explaining. What I wanted to know that you, as a judge, know very well that if the file is with you nothing is done at the court on the level where there should be an action. And that was the aim of my question, to know what, if there was any serious reason for you to have this file for two months, as you told us. You explained, thank you, that there were no such reasons. Last week, you were explaining us that removal of the Mice was done under certain regulation. I just wanted to know -- and you were not able to identify this regulation. I just wanted to know if during the weekend by chance if you don't remember what sort of regulation it was.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought about this. And there is a decision here on the organisation and headquarters of penitentiary correctional institutions, but I didn't bring that law with me. This was a decision dated the 12th of May, and it says, "In departments for detainees, within the framework of a penitentiary correctional institution, the provisions of Articles 201 to 205 of the law on criminal proceedings of the SFRY are applied." I didn't have that law, so I can't remember offhand what the provision of those articles indicate. Probably that detention should be served in court and the detention units may be governed by a certain bylaw so the minister of justice is authorised to regulate this. We have taken over the regulations from the former Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. And my last question, as you said you are now -- you work as a private lawyer, can you tell me, have you been employed by this Court?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to raise that, Your Honours, at the end. He has. It's a matter I raised last week, and I want to come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. So that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. In the meantime, I suppose he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm currently working on the Krajisnik case as a legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: When did you start this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started working in that case in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And in what position are you working?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now working as legal assistant, legal advisor, consultant. So I'm not the lead counsel, I'm not co-counsel, but I am the legal assistant or advisor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour, I think we may as well deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Do you mind, Judge Janu, if Ms. Korner intervenes at this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on the subject. Can I hand Your Honour the directive of the 30th of July 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my last question is, from the evidence here, from today's evidence, we could see that you were a close cooperator with Mr. Milan Trbojevic when he was a minister of justice. Can you tell the Chamber what, Mr. Trbojevic, if you know, what is he doing now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not cooperate with Mr. Trbojevic when he was minister of justice. I was a lawyer at the time, in 1999. I met Mr. Trbojevic during the war in 1994 when he, too, was a lawyer. But we never cooperated closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: All right. But you know him well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as well as any others. We're a small country. All the attorneys know one another. We have our assembly meetings and other encounters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. And you said, if I remember -- recall well, that Mr. Trbojevic introduced you to Mr. Brdjanin, and you said you didn't know him before. And just you saw him on television and on media. Do you recall what Mr. Brdjanin was telling on television and media at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year are you referring to, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember assembly meetings when Mr. Brdjanin took the floor, at people's assemblies, when he spoke like all the other deputies. It was difficult to follow the media because there was no electricity until October in 1992. But until the war started, I followed regularly assembly meetings that were telecast. Seven days ago, there was a report about the trial here, and some excerpts were broadcast from Mr. Brdjanin's speeches. And I think a rally was shown which he addressed on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My interest was if you remember, if you recall something that was said in 1992. I thought maybe as a judge with a deep sense for justice that something might strike you, surprise you at his speeches. But you don't recall obviously, so that's all my questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Taya, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a few last questions for you, sir. And I think I will try and refer you first to one of the incidents that you testified about earlier on today before the break. And that is your handing over of the Mice court file to the police, to the MUP. When did this actually happen, which year?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened in 1996, on the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on the 15th of August of 1996, what was your position in the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy minister of justice and liaison officer with the Tribunal on behalf of the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who were your immediate superiors in the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was the minister of justice in August of 1996, 15th of August 1996?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Branko Petric [as interpreted], or Marko Arsovic was before him, and then Mr. Peric. No, I'm sorry, Marko Arsovic, because he was travelled to The Hague. So I beg your pardon, it was Marko Arsovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After receiving the request to hand over the file by MUP and before handing over the file, the court file, to MUP, did you consult your superior, the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. That is why it was left in the protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you get the go-ahead from the minister of justice to hand the file to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did get the go ahead, since it was handed over and signed by the MUP. So I think approval was given because one couldn't do anything with the approval of the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when you previously said, upon being asked by Ms. Korner and also by myself how come a previous judge agrees to hand over a court file to the police without raising any questions, you told me "I wouldn't dare." Why wouldn't you dare if it was actually the minister who had taken the decision, who had agreed for the transfer of the file?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you why in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did not tell us why in private session. You said a lot of things in private session, but not this. When I asked you the question, you, as a judge, would have known better, you as a judge shouldn't have accepted to hand over this file, a court file, to the executive, to the police, your answer was not "I had instructions from above to hand it over"; your answer was "I wouldn't dare." "I didn't dare."

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why did you tell me "I didn't dare" and not "Judge, it wasn't me who decided to hand over the file but it was the minister"? You could have told me that, if that was the truth. But you didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you think there's some kind of a protocol behind all this. Somebody just -- you go to the minister and you say: "They're asking for this file," and he says: "Hand it over." There's no protocol or official procedure. I had more than 500 court files in my office. If there's a crime committed, then it has to be copied and handed over to the Tribunal. This wasn't the only court file that was in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I suggest to you that none of the other 499 court files dealt with something as serious as this court file on the Mice group. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other cases, there were files on crimes committed against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. When you consulted your immediate superior, the minister, did you point out to him that it was absolutely irregular for a court file to be handed over by the Ministry of Justice, who was in temporary possession of that file, to the police, to another ministry? Did you point that out to the minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We all knew that it was irregular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this was kind of a conspiracy between you and the minister of justice to do something that you knew was irregular?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the problem, if the file is handed over and the court was informed about it. This happened in other cases, too. Then the file is returned. It is common knowledge that the MUP had files, and they did do some operational work and checks through those files. In addition to this file, there was another file in Teslic. It is a criminal report of the opposite side submitted by Doboj against Banja Luka security centre and against the police in Teslic, also for killings. And that file was also used by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did it disappear?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't been informed about that file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the Mice court file did disappear, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that it was handed over to the OTP in 2001. I searched for it, and in the office for relations with the Tribunal I was told that the file had been found and handed over to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's change to something different. You will recall that last Friday I read you from the part -- an extract from the minutes of the Teslic Municipal Assembly held on the 20th of August of 1992, and particularly the part which reports the speech made by Dusan Kuzmanovic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
