utterances.text: Just to make sure that you will understand my next question, I'm going to read out again that part. It's a few lines. Mr. Kuzmanovic said: "Mr. Jokic's statement that the Mices were in Teslic as some sort of paramilitary formation is not accurate. That group had official authorisation from the higher military command to conduct mobilisation and set up civilian authority in the municipality. Everyone in the authority was made aware of it. The activities of the Teslic SJB were under the patronage of the crisis staff. The crisis staff was aware of the operational group activities while the police only had the role of guides in these activities. The conflict with the operational group from Doboj ensued when there was mention of crimes in which the political and economic leadership of Teslic allegedly participated." Now, my question to you is this: If Mr. Kuzmanovic is right, if the arrival of the Mice in Teslic had nothing to do with paramilitary formations but was, indeed, an execution of decision which was taken at the highest political levels and with the patronage of the crisis staff, how would you account for the decision to arrest the members of this Mice group? What happened? What made the authorities arrest the Mice group members?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think because they had committed these crimes and executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware that the entire population of Teslic were clamouring for the arrest and summary trials of these Mice group members? And when I say "the entire population," I mean Serbs and non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they were in conflict with the entire population of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that there was a lot of pressure on the president of the municipality, amongst others, to ensure that the members of the Mice group were brought to justice? Were stopped and brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that because I wasn't in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware that a meeting took place between the president of the Teslic Municipality and the authorities in Banja Luka, particularly the SJB and also the military in Banja Luka, to organise the arrest of the Mice group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't informed of that, no. Did you say in Banja Luka, that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the meeting took place in Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other meeting taking place anywhere else in which it was decided -- the arrest of the Mice group was decided?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it had all been decided in Teslic. I know that the chief of the centre in Doboj went to the Teslic when the conflicts broke out. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who arrested the Mice group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police, the local police from Teslic and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you do confirm today that with the exception of one, all the members of the Mice group were from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was one other person who wasn't from Doboj, upon reading it a second time. I think he was number four, the person under number four. Yes, I found that when I analysed this later, number four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I put it to you that this whole affair, the Mice group, gave rise to great discord and arm-wrestling between Doboj and Teslic at the time, great confrontation, great discord, and a show of strength between Doboj and Teslic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did the confrontation become more acute when it became known in Teslic that the members of the Mice group had been brought over from Banja Luka and were released?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. What I do know is that we had good cooperation in the court, and the court functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. But that was not --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the Teslic and Doboj courts, that there was no confrontation there between us judges in that respect. And I assume that the confrontation was great between the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am going to read out to you an extract from a report. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P388, please. An extract from a report drawn up by the war staff of Teslic Municipality and addressed to the Assembly and government of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, and the Banja Luka Security Services Centre. And this is dated the 4th of July 1992. On the -- I would imagine it's either the end of the first page or the beginning of the second page, there is a paragraph which starts "unfortunately, sympathisers of those arrested..." Have you found it? It's eight paragraphs from the end.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. "Unfortunately," it says, "sympathisers," et cetera, et cetera. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. "Unfortunately sympathisers of those arrested located mostly on Mount Ozren reacted to the arrests by threatening to fire Howitzers at Teslic from Ozren and retaliating against the people who organised their arrests. Relations between these two Serbian towns of Teslic and Doboj became so strained that it could have all turned into a conflict between them. Warnings were issued that the corridor for Serbia was not valid for Teslic as well as a series of other accusations." And again, I take you to the very end of this document before the -- it says: "We thank you in advance for your understanding." There's another paragraph that says: "Because of the specific nature of this situation, particularly the relations between Teslic and Doboj, we are sending a copy of this report to the highest state organs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." How bad was this confrontation and this discord between Doboj and Teslic at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is correct. I don't believe that there was any major conflict or confrontation. And it seems to me to be ridiculous that somebody would target anybody some 40 kilometres away with some Howitzers. What's that got to do with anything? I can see all the addressees, who it was sent to, but nobody contacted me with respect to this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But my question was --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I read out these excerpts from this report because I want to hear from your own mouth your personal assessment of how bad the situation was when it came to relations between Doboj and Teslic at the time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is -- how shall I put that? This was rather inflated and exaggerated, that that's not actually how things were, because this is how it was in Teslic and Doboj and Mount Ozren: You had one army, it was the 1st Krajina Corps with one commander. And one commander can replace a commander in Doboj and Teslic. That comes under his competency. That is why I don't think the situation was the kind of having a large confrontation. A confrontation can be created by the army and the police. They're the only ones with weapons that can make a confrontation, so I don't think this was actually how things stood. Yes, the relations were strained. I heard about that. But the balance of power was that the Doboj people didn't go to Teslic, and Teslic people didn't go to Doboj. But I don't think it was as tense as this for a confrontation to have arisen. I'm not quite sure that it reflects the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And after the release of the Mice group members in July, towards the end of July of 1992, did the situation improve between Doboj and Teslic, or did it get worse?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. Those relations lasted until the autumn. That is to say, relations deteriorated until the autumn. Actually, it wasn't a deterioration of relations in that respect. What is was was that some people had lost their lives there, from Doboj and Teslic in the conflicts, young policemen, young police officers. And the chief of the centre from Doboj, the police chief went to a meeting, and there was a fight. He was beaten up and had to be taken to hospital. So I think the conflict and confrontation was in that respect, between the police. That was where the tension lay, rather than a confrontation between the army and perhaps the political authorities. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1945, please. Are you aware that the situation deteriorated to such an extent that General Mladic, Ratko Mladic himself, had to intervene to try and put some order where it belonged? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if it's in English, please let him have it in B/C/S. The backside of it is in B/C/S. Please read it out.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read it out loud, all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre of the Security Services Centre, the sector of the station for public security, Banja Luka, the operative workers, Radulovic, Stjepanovic, Sainovic, the date is the 30th of October 1992, strictly confidential, just for internal use, for internal use only. It is an official note. "In the course of today's day, in the area of Teslic, General Mladic spent the day with respect to solving the problem between political structures in Teslic and Doboj. On the occasion he gave full support to the political structures in Teslic and especially to the present leadership of the public security station of Teslic, emphasising that he would personally see to it that the previously replaced officers who had been appointed to posts of leadership again by Minister Stanisic be banned from entering the public security station. "He offered the chief of the public security station physical security if he wasn't able to provide security for the police station itself. He also said that he would support the deputies in the municipal assembly of Teslic at the Assembly of Republika Srpska, and that he would strive in favour of having the decision by the municipal decision to join up the Banja Luka region be verified. Finally, however, in addition to that the centre of services in Doboj sent a telegram today asking for the urgent handover between the present leadership of the public security station and the newly appointed leadership, or rather the previously replaced individuals. "We feel that this untactical move creates even greater revolt towards the public security station of Doboj and the overall Doboj region, the situation in Teslic is very complex, and there is the danger of an armed conflict breaking between the sympathisers of the previously replaced and present leadership of the public security station of Teslic which enjoys the support of the majority. According to our information, this insistence on the Doboj service is designed to mask the large number of crimes that have been perpetrated by members of the active and reserve formation of the centre of security services, three or four months ago. And this has been sent to the chief of the public security station," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if I take you to three to four months before October, where does that get us? And when the last paragraph refers to members of the active and reserve force of the Doboj CSB, would that refer to --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that refer to part or some of the members of the Mice group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so because I think -- I see a conflict between the replaced leadership and the new leadership, so that refers to them, I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically this strictly confidential Security Services Centre document attributes to the Doboj CSB this -- these attempts to hide, to conceal the various crimes that some of its members had committed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I see that this was compiled by the CSB service of Banja Luka, and I can also see from this note that it is a conflict between the former leadership of the public security station of Teslic, and the new leadership, and the conflict with the CSB centre of Doboj. That's what I said earlier on, that most probably, the conflict continued between the police themselves mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree that way back in July of 1992 when the Mice members were arrested, the Doboj CSB would have also been insistent to procure their release in order to be able to conceal the crimes that they had committed? Would you agree with that? This insistence did not arise in October, but it was also there way back in July.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read out the letter that the Security Services Centre of Doboj sent on the 17th of July requesting that they be released and that the court should continue with its proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is your position that subsequent to the arrest of the Mice group and until their release you were not the subject of this insistence on the part of the CSB? No pressure was brought to bear on you to ensure the release of these members of the Mice group? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. And Judge Kovacevic is aware of that. Nobody exerted any pressure on me ever, and you could -- can question all the witnesses to bear that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was there any insistence at all that you are aware of in Doboj at the time by the population or by any other quarters from the population of Doboj insisting on the arrest or rearrest of the Mice group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Doboj, no. I didn't hear about that ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware that Judge Kovacevic had a great amount of pressure brought to bear on him by the military and also by the security services in favour of the Mice group from the very moment they came under his jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that the police and army did contact Judge Kovacevic and that when they were released, he agreed to the request made by the military command. Now, whether there was any oral pressure he didn't convey that to me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you since then been made aware that there was a tremendous amount of pressure on Judge Kovacevic at the time to -- not to proceed with the investigations and to have the Mice group released immediately? Have you ever come across any documents? Have you ever been made aware of this pressure, at least the allegation of this pressure?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown again please Exhibit 1938, which he saw last Friday. And Mr. Neskovic, could you go, please, to paragraph numbered 6. It would be on the second or the third page, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- this is the same document we showed you last Friday, and it is a report on initiating criminal proceedings against members of the military police and the Security Services Centre in Doboj and problems relating to the actions of judicial organ submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor in Teslic dated 28 of July and transmitted to the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of Justice, to the Ministry of the Interior, and to the Ministry of National Defence. In paragraph 6, it is reported here that after the investigating judge heard the accused and ordered that they be remanded in custody, the defence attorneys of the accused, military organs, and relatives of the accused began exerting pressure on the court. Defence counsel objected to the detention order stressing that the space in which the accused were put was not a prison, that conditions for keeping them in custody as prescribed by law were not met, and that there were beaten and sick detainees whose life was at risk in such circumstances. It goes on as follows: "The command of the Doboj operations group sent a letter to this office" - that's to the office of the Prosecutor - "and the lower court on the 11th of July 1992 requesting that the accused Slavuljica be immediately handed over to the military security services of this group. The letter was personally brought by Security Officer Maksimovic. Dario Slavuljica is the son of reserve Captain First Class Mirko Slavuljica from Doboj. The letter underlined that 'no one has the right to play with the fate of a Serbian soldier,' 'we cannot allow him to be treated in this way.' As proof of the lack of principle on the part of the command, we wish to note that in that letter the command showed not interest at all in the other soldiers." And then it goes on as follows: "Several times the defence attorneys stressed to the investigating judge that 'this will not end well,' that 'the attack on Teslic from Mount Ozren was prepared by the military' and that we were also on a list. The brother of the first defendant Miroslav Pijunovic issued a similar open threat to the investigating judge. "On the 17th of July 1992, the operations group command submitted to the investigating judge a letter requesting that all the servicemen listed therein be released so that they could join in the fight in the Doboj, Teslic, and Tesanj areas. On the same day, the Doboj Security Services Centre requested that the rest of the men, allegedly its employees, be released for the same reason." And the Office of the Prosecutor in Teslic concludes this part of the report by saying: "We deem this kind of behaviour of the Doboj operations group command and the Doboj Security Services Centre towards the work of judicial organs in Teslic an inappropriate form of pressure which gives the criminal case additional political weight. The military command does not even want to know with which crimes its members are charged and is not showing a readiness to assist the court in shedding light on the whole case. The same can be applied to the security services centre in Doboj." Would you agree with what is contained in that report, in this part of the report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am informed of this letter of the 17th of July. I know about it. I have the letter. And the security centre Doboj, yes, but I don't know any of this. It's not known to me. Probably the possibility for that exists, but Peric didn't inform me this. Neither did the investigating judge, Mr. Kovacevic. And as I've already said, I told you last time, that this piece of information is dated the 28th of July 1992, and on the 21st, the prosecutor proposed that eight persons be released. So that means that he succumbed to the pressure most probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put to you that when it was obvious that Judge Kovacevic was doing his best not to succumb to the pressure that was forthcoming from Doboj, and took steps to ensure the detention of the detainees in Banja Luka, you brought your weight in and put your own kind of pressure in support of the other authorities from Doboj to ensure that more pressure will be brought to bear on Judge Kovacevic. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can talk to Judge Kovacevic. Had I brought any pressure to bear on him, I should certainly have put it down in the information, prosecutor. I never said a word to Kovacevic to release or not to release. I always let him make the decisions. I didn't meddle in that. You can call Mr. Kovacevic, Your Honour, talk to him freely. But I exerted no pressure on the judge myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put it to you that Judge Kovacevic made sure or tried to avoid all this pressure by making sure that the detainees were kept in Banja Luka and that he was the person who decided to have them transferred to Banja Luka. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've said that I don't know how they were transferred or transported to Banja Luka. Why did he inform me that they had been transferred to Banja Luka? Did he want to distance himself from that, dissociate himself? Why did the judge let that happen? He could have come to Banja Luka, say: "I'm the investigating judge and I'm not going to allow the prisoners to go to Doboj." And I say in the interview, I say that I never discussed this with him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did the Witness still have P1938 in front of him, usher? Could you go to paragraph 9, please, paragraph 9. This is again the prosecutor in Teslic reporting to higher authorities. "Since its start, the course of criminal proceedings has been accompanied with the problem of inadequate accommodation of the detainees about which the defence counsel raised justified objections. The detainees were accommodated in the same room in the Kardijal Hotel, although they had to be separated in order to prevent their collusion given that they were co-perpetrators. For this reason, in consultation with the chief of the SJB, the investigating judge" - that's Judge Kovacevic - "ordered on the 16th of July 1992 that the detainees be placed in the district prison in Banja Luka. All the detainees were transferred to the district prison in Banja Luka on the 17th of July 1992." I put it to you that Judge Kovacevic had no intention at all to see these people free and running in the streets; it was only you who made sure they were free three days after.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Why did he release three of them, then, on the 16th? And secondly, it wasn't for three days. They were released on the 24th. I'm claiming that it was on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you have -- you are --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by the judge, yes, on the 17th of July. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're very capable of running at a tangent in your attempts not to answer the question. I'm not referring to those three or to the other one who was hospitalised. I'm referring to the others. They were sent to Banja Luka not because Judge Kovacevic wanted their release; they were sent to Banja Luka for other purposes. But you stepped in to ensure that they did not remain in Banja Luka, and you stepped in again to ensure that once they were out of Banja Luka they were free men running in the streets barely three days after their transfer to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Your Honour. If I knew that Kovacevic would release them later on, I would never have requested their movement from Banja Luka, even if that was contrary to the law. You can talk to Kovacevic and ask him. I never used my influence to have them freed. If Kovacevic had not taken the decision on the 21st, they would never have been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it right --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. But this report is written by the public prosecutor. I must say again that on the 21st, the public prosecutor proposed to the investigating judge their release. So the motive must be sought for the prosecutor. I have no contact with the prosecutor. The prosecutor is an independent organ, and he should be asked by he did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was there a change in the prosecutor? Was the prosecutor changed at some point in July?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, which month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Teslic, was the prosecutor changed in July?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think it was the same prosecutor throughout the war. He was in his position throughout the war, and so was Kovacevic. I am not aware of any change of prosecutor ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a schizophrenic prosecutor who does one thing and writes another? Why would you think a prosecutor is writing what he is writing in this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he compiled this report correctly. I just think he added a little more than he should have, and he's probably covering up for himself because he proposed that they be released on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put it to you that -- again, I'm going to repeat the question. Would Judge, Kovacevic perhaps in a last-ditch attempt try to leave undone, that is, by retaining a part -- some members of the Mice group still in detention after releasing the rest, what he left undone, your court ensured that it would be done. That is correct, too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The prosecutor made the proposal for their release here, too. When this was being decided I wasn't even in Doboj. I found this 15 days ago in the archives of the higher prosecutor's office. If the judge should have retained anyone in detention, then it was these men who are mentioned in the decision on the investigation. And the judge says, "very well, five persons have admitted that they participated in the executions following orders of a superior military commander. The other persons did not confess, and they did not participate." So this last group that stayed behind are not one of the five. Those five were released on the proposal of the prosecutor on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, you were shown some documents that in actual fact you brought with you earlier on today relating to the undertaking signed by some of the detainees --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I make this absolutely clear. He may have brought them with them, but we had them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We didn't take them from him, but we had them originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. About the request to be released to have a bath, and the undertaking to show up in court on the 20th. Now, this contact was made on the 18th of July, I take it, from the Banja Luka prison directly with you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who made the contact -- who made the contact and with whom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was by the prison authorities of Doboj who contacted the prison authorities in Banja Luka. I had no contact with the prison or anyone else. They went to Banja Luka, the prison authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who referred to you the desire or the request of these detainees to be released in order to go and have a bath?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The workers employed in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which prison?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They passed on to me -- from the Doboj prison. The conversation was as follows: That they were going to Banja Luka to see whether they would be handed over those prisoners. And then I said I'm asking that you provide guarantees that they will come to prison, and they said if that is all right, can we let them have a bath. And I said yes, but I have to be certain that they will come back because I asked for those prisoners to be taken over from Jovo. And then each one of them filled in these forms. The following week, they brought those forms to me. I certified them with my signature and put them in the archives of the court where they are at present. And that is why I brought them with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are approaching the end. I want to know exactly when you ceased being prosecutor and became acting president of the high court in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to give you an exact date, Your Honour, because they don't have a record of this up there. You see, I was in the records of the prosecutor's office up until the 31st of July. And I have a certificate to that event. It means that that is where I received my personal income. And I was elected president of the district court on the 20th of July, or at least that is the date of the decision. So I think I was already acting president in the first half of July. Before me, there was another acting president. He was also in an acting capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you were formally approved on the 20th of July, how long had you been acting? Would you agree that you had been acting, say, the previous 20 days, from the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around then, in the first half. But I don't have the date in my working booklet, nor in the court is there a date recorded. So I think from the beginning of July, maybe the 10th. Between the 10th and the 15th. Anyway, in the first half of July. And before me there was also another person who was also the acting president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you were formally appointed president on the 20th of July 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the day you were celebrating, the same day the Mice group returnees from Doboj were celebrating. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a strange coincidence, Your Honour, because Jovo Rosic was elected judge in Banja Luka. I have the Official Gazette. It so happens all judges were elected on the 20th of July. You can check this, election of judges in Banja Luka. They were also elected on the 20th of July. All this was published in the Official Gazette. We didn't even know because there were no communications, so all these things reached us 10 or 15 days later. This is the Official Gazette. Election of judges in Banja Luka, Jovo Rosic on the 20th of July. Then election of judges in Doboj, again, on the 20th. So it's a pure coincidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Neskovic, in this whole tragedy, you appear on the stage three times.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first time is 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th of July 1992. The beginning, you're still acting president. At the end, you are president of the high court. In between, you are the person who procured the release of these criminals. That's the first time you appear on stage. The second time you appear on stage is when your colleague, Mr. Kovacevic, sends these detainees to Banja Luka. And you, on the basis of your jurisdictional claims, as you put it, procure their return to Doboj. And at the same time, give your blessing to the -- what Ms. Korner put it to you, provisional release. The third time you appear on stage is when the MUP ask for this file, the court file, and instead of keeping the file and giving them a copy you give them the original file and, guess what? Just vanishes, disappears into thin air. How clean do you come out of this affair, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't know in 1992 that in 1996 I would be a deputy minister and a liaison officer. This is just mere coincidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your answer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think with that answer we can send you back --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, not quite, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have something else, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do. Your Honour will recall that on Friday, Mr. Neskovic was producing from his folder a number of documents. And he announced - this is page 17 - that the prosecutor had the document, the decision to conduct an investigation on the 11th of July. And you asked: "How come you know or you tell us that you know which documents the Prosecution already has?" Answer: "I apologise. I know because this decision on conducting an investigation which I have has the markings of the Prosecution. I borrowed this from another case because I was involved in another case." Your Honour, Mr. Neskovic was assigned as co-counsel in the Krajisnik case as of sometime in -- yes, January 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 16th of January. Come the debacle that took place, as Your Honours will recall, last summer, Mr. Brashich was removed in May, but kept on so that he could hand it -- gather the papers and hand it over. Mr. Neskovic stated on the 13th of May, he gave a description of his role, and it was decided that he had insufficient experience in criminal law as a result of which the assignment was withdrawn on the 30th of July. And Your Honour will see that the last order from the Registrar was: "In accordance with the decision of the Registrar dated the 2nd of May 2003, and the letter, Mr. Brashich shall prepare a complete dossier of the status of the case, complete the transfer of documents and materials to Mr. Stewart, the new counsel and advise him of any pending issues." From the moment Mr. Neskovic's assignment was withdrawn, the Krajisnik case has the same measures in this case that we do, namely that all documents in his possession must be handed to legal counsel, and in this case lead counsel had to hand them over to Mr. Stewart. I invite Your Honours to find out what he is doing with a copy of a Prosecution document at this stage and whether he still retains any other Prosecution documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, do you have a statement in this regard? Because you have been telling us that you are legal assistant in the Krajisnik -- he said consultant, legal assistant, legal advisor. He used three different terms. While it seems that his only position was that as co-counsel, and that has been withdrawn. So what's the position with regard to your status in the Krajisnik case, if at all; and secondly, with regard to the documents? Because if you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- The Krajisnik case officially --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I received instructions from you to testify, you said in the interests of truth. I understood it to mean that I had to mention every document, every note that I saw. And I saw this decision in another case, and that is why I wanted to inform you about it. But I didn't mention it in my testimony at all. When Mr. Stewart was appointed on August the 1st, I am working for him. I can't be precise as regards the term, whether it was a legal consultant, a legal advisor. I'm still in the team. I have five investigators. 90 per cent of the documents from the Prosecution are in the possession of the investigators because we are preparing the Defence case, and we have the documents. These are just documents that the previous lawyer had to return to Stewart, that was in the States. The rest of the documents, the copies of the documents are with us. I'm still a member of the team. If I'm not, this is the first I hear of it. I was working until the end of last week as now it is the Prosecution case that is being produced in court. It would be disrespect towards the Court if I said if I had a document in my hands and didn't inform you about it. I wanted to tell you that I read a document and I had an important sentence -- I found an important sentence in it, and I didn't dare read it until I received permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is retaining you? Who is paying you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Tribunal, as a legal assistant for the work I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you ever received any communication from the Tribunal subsequent or following the 30th of July 2003 stating "Mr. Neskovic, you know that your assignment as co-counsel has been withdrawn. You are being approved as legal assistant or anything of the sort"? Have you received any communication from the --

utterances.speaker: GORAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. But I have been informed by the lead counsel what my position is. He talked to me in September when he came here, and he gave me assignments for me to do. I have five investigators working for me. I'm working on this every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I invite Your Honours to remit the matter for investigation by the Registrar. But my one concern is that documents which have strict measures being applied to them for the use to which they may be made are clearly not -- in this case, Mr. Neskovic is using it for a completely different purpose. It may be if Your Honour wishes to remit this to the Krajisnik Trial Chamber for dealing with it, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime, can I ask you, Ms. Korner, to tender this as an exhibit, the letter -- Registrar's letter to the witness in the Momcilo Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't intending to because it doesn't really arise out of his evidence here. It's arises how he's in possession of a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me make a proces verbale. I'm going to make an order that in the course of last Friday's, as well as today's testimony by Mr. Goran Neskovic, it emerged that he is claiming -- that the witness is claiming that he is assigned as legal assistant in the Krajisnik case. In particular, in today's testimony, he confirmed that in September, Mr. Nicholas Stewart --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. September or the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or the beginning of October, Mr. Stewart, Nicholas, who replaced him as co-counsel --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: , Your Honour, he was replaced. The Registry replaced him before Mr. Stewart took over, or at the time, and the decision was made by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Ms. Korner. Particularly in today's testimony, he confirmed that either in late September or the beginning of October, he was appointed by Mr. Stewart to render services as legal assistant -- legal assistant, that he has a team of five persons working under him carrying out investigations, that in this context, he and his team are in possession of the necessary documentation in the Krajisnik team, and that above all he is being paid for his services by this Tribunal. The Trial Chamber has been asked by Ms. Korner, lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, to refer this matter to the Registrar for any further investigations that might be necessary; and in particular, in view of the fact that the witness has made use in this case of a document which he came in possession of in the Krajisnik case and of which he should not be still in possession if he no longer has a locus tandi in the Krajisnik case. This would also be the case should he be, in addition, in possession of other documents. For this purpose, the Trial Chamber instructs the Deputy Registrar to identify the parts of the transcript from today's sitting and that of last Friday and have them forwarded to the Registrar of this Tribunal, together with this order for any further investigations that the Registrar might deem fit. As you realise, in my country, I dictate, so I was trying to keep the pace that I would keep in my country when you have stenographers taking down the... So Mr. Neskovic, the Trial Chamber does not require your presence any further. On behalf of the Trial Chamber and on behalf of the Tribunal, on behalf of Judge Janu and Judge Taya, I should like to thank you for having come over and give your testimony following the issue of a summons to that effect by the Trial Chamber and as a witness of the Trial Chamber. On behalf of everyone present also, I should like to wish you a safe journey back home. You will receive all the assistance that you require to facilitate your return to ex-Yugoslavia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else before we rise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes. I was wondering whether Your Honour wanted to deal today with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Defence exhibits, plus for ages and ages, I have been wanting to put in Dzafic's redacted statement that shows the acronyms, so I'd like to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I don't know if you were present last week when we discussed the matter of the documents, your proposed exhibits. So are you in a position to discuss that today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I probably don't have anything -- I mean, Ms. Korner wants to tell you orally her objections rather than in writing. I probably won't have any response, because I expect you'll treat --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman has been aware since the 11th of this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why is she interrupting me? Can you ask her that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's still Monday morning, so you may have to be indulgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe that's what it is. What I was getting ready to say is I probably won't have any response because I expect you will treat my exhibits the same way you treated the Prosecutor's exhibits, and that is you'll admit them all in decide in the course of your what weight you're going to give them, if any. And if that's not the case, if you're going to change that rule, then I will have some things to say, but I doubt that you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no change of rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go straight away to argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you'll have to rise, Your Honour. We've had over an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, how long will this debate last?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't know. Your Honour, I have some quite major objections to these things, including General Talic's so-called statement, which I don't know if Your Honours have read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it. Let's have a break of 25 minutes, and then we try to conclude on this matter within -- by quarter to 2.00. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I start by handing in, please, finally the Dzafic list of acronyms. It's a redacted statement, as Your Honours ordered. Mr. Ackerman's had a copy. There are three copies, four, five. And could that be made Exhibit 2734. 2-7-3-4 -- 3-5? What's 4? 5, thank you. It's redacted so it just shows the list of acronyms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I turn now to the exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- that Mr. Ackerman proposes to tender in bulk. I have very few objections, but I would like to put them before Your Honours, or objections to a few exhibits. Your Honour, I did object to DB77, but as I understand it, Mr. Ackerman withdrew that document, and DB90 to 92 also withdrawn. Your Honour, can I turn next then to DB229 to 239 and 241 to 251. This is not an objection as such. It is a request, before Your Honours admit it, that we be told where these documents come from. Your Honour, there's nothing to indicate on the schedule. There are an extraordinary set of documents. They seem to be something to do with Trnopolje. What they're supposed to be or where they come from, no indication is given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop there for the moment. Mr. Ackerman, are you in a position to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they came from a person whose name I do not know, but I can find out, who has custody of all the documents from Trnopolje, or at least the documents that are in front of you. We were wishing to bring that person as a witness and that person refused to come. And the documents are a little confusing without some testimony to explain to you what they are. But they have to do with the daily workings of Trnopolje. Whether Your Honours would find them of any value without the testimony accompanying them, I don't know. They are a little bit vague without it. But that's the best I can do with regard to those. I can find that name if that becomes important. I can get that within 24 hours, I think, because one of my investigators knows the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially if he was intended to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the difficulty. I don't know how we're supposed to treat all this or how Your Honours -- if Mr. Ackerman admits that they are confusing. Well, Your Honour, perhaps if Mr. Ackerman by tomorrow can supply us with the name of the person and we can make some investigations ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, I totally sympathise with Ms. Korner's concern about these documents, and the name is not going to make them any clearer. I really think without the testimony, they're of no value, and I think for that reason I'll withdraw them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So these have been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's 229 to 239 and 241 to 251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Inclusive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we then move then please next to 288 and 289. Again, Your Honour, these are -- it's the same problem. It's part of a newspaper article, it appears, looking at the original. It appears (Redacted). Your Honour, can I go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. So we're dealing with DB335 and also 343. The Trial Chamber's position, having heard you, in particular, Mr. Ackerman, and with background of submissions made earlier throughout these two years with regard to AID, I think our position is that these two documents do not help us in any way to improve our assessment. So it's up to you to decide whether you would like to retain them or not, particularly since you did not pursue the matter of the AID further than you actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think I'm being invited to withdraw them, Your Honour. And if they are of no use to you, then I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as db344 was concerned, that was one I had notified my objection, and you entered it as an exhibit with BT-94, who was asked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Except, Your Honour, as I pointed it out, this was purportedly a -- an account given by a man called Sendic, and that if they wanted this evidence in, if it wasn't being tendered for the truth of the contents, if they wanted the evidence in, Mr. Sendic could be called. Your Honours let it go in, and BT-94 was then asked about it, part of it, and he said, "I don't know anything about it at all." So Your Honour, I am repeating my objection. It has no admissible value in that nobody could speak about one of the things that Mr. Sendic said, and if it's being purportedly put in for the truth of the contents of what Mr. Sendic says, then it's inadmissible. So Your Honour, I repeat my objection to that. Your Honours let it in. BT-94 was asked about part of that article, and he said, "I don't know the first thing about that." So what's the value to Your Honours of this particular document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think -- we really do seem to be changing the rules. The value is the same as newspaper articles the Prosecution has put in that we don't even know what publication they're from. You've let all that in. I've objected in detail to Prosecution exhibits, and on every occasion you said we note your objections and admit all the exhibits. Now I'm being asked to reply to all of these objections as if Defence exhibits come in on a different rule than Prosecution exhibits, and I don't think it's fair. I don't know what 344 is for sure, because it's not on the list that Ms. Korner sent me of exhibits she was going to object to in any event. So I'm a little bit at a handicap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, can I just -- not right, I sent a second email including that on my list on the 12th of the 2nd. In any event, we had a discussion about this when BT-94 was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the person who was one of the cofounders of the SDS who then felt he couldn't agree any more with the policy and politics of the SDS. He tried to speak, and he was -- made a speech. He was not allowed. He was actually ostracised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honour. It isn't. This is the man who was a paramilitary who then became some kind of a minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. I'm mixing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's different. And the simple, simple thing is that this is evidence that Mr. Ackerman is tendering only to bolster up his own case. As far as we know, this man is alive and well. The article was written in 2002. And this was a man who could have been called as a witness. He wasn't. If the only reason this article is being put in is for the truth of what this man asserts, our application would be it doesn't go in. If Mr. Ackerman wants it, his case is still open. We want that witness called so we can cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think she was talking about the Patriot article. And again , Your Honours, there are numerous articles in this case from the Prosecution, where people are making statements that the Prosecution is relying on, including this fellow -- there's not even newspaper articles, this fellow Milos. They're relying on all kinds of statements from Milos. They could have called him had they wanted to, they found out what his name was. They didn't. So are we going throw out all the Milos statements? I mean, are we going to have a new rule or not? If we're not going to have a new rule, we ought to just stop this and you should let in these exhibits, except the ones I have agreed are not going in. This argument just strikes me as being contrary to everything we've done in this case so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, now I'm aware which document we're talking about. I was mixing it up with something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go on further, it's not the same thing. The Milos documents, yes, we do now know who Milos is. We didn't at the time, we do now know. The Milos documents, the objection was because they were unsigned. And indeed, Mr. Ackerman, much to my amazement, given his objection to this, has put in a number of further documents as part of his exhibits from Milos. Your Honour, this is something that have written after the time. These are not documents that came into existence at the time, and the only reason, as I repeat, that Mr. Ackerman is trying to put this in is because he's going to use that evidence as truth of what this man said. And I am simply saying he's alive, he wrote this in 2002, if Mr. Ackerman wants that put in, he can call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Next document. Yes, Mr. Ackerman -- I beg your pardon. I apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is important. It's a memoir written by somebody who was there at the time. It's not the sole source of information. There's huge information in this case showing that Mr. Brdjanin was opposed to paramilitaries and opposed to all the things that this guy says he was opposed to. So it's just confirmatory of what has been made, I think, abundantly clear in this case already. But I think it's an important confirmation because it comes from somebody who was very much on the inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman has just made my point for me. This is a point of strong dispute in the case. He says it's important, and it's confirmatory. I don't accept there's any real evidence that Mr. Brdjanin was opposed to Serbian paramilitaries. But if this is being put in as confirmatory, then I wish to be able to cross-examine. Your Honour, that's -- you've heard the objections on that. And I'll move to the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, 345, Your Honour -- actually my words to Mr. Ackerman, I take it this is a joke. This is the so-called statement signed by Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that it may be that Your Honours can see how much value it has, I take the objection in principle. Your Honour, we know absolutely nothing about the circumstances in which he came to sign it. It was dated December. If it was proposed in December 1992, that in some form or another the Defence would wish his evidence in, despite his condition, then that should have been made known to the Court and to the Prosecution well in advance, and certainly before his death took place in, whenever it was, in March. There are all sorts of rules relating to this which Mr. Ackerman hasn't troubled to address. At the moment, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, what's your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be quite brief. Very early in the case, even before the trial started, Mr. Talic expressed his wish to testify to the effect of what is contained that statement. As you know, then became terminally ill. We were hoping that his condition would improve enough that we could have him as a witness. We weren't able to. Just as a matter of cautionary -- a cautionary matter, we had this statement taken from him at a time when he was -- knew he was facing death. And so we think it is -- may be admissible as a dying declaration, although it doesn't fit every requirement of a dying declaration, and I'm not going to argue that it does. But that would be the basis under which it would be admitted and the only basis under which it could be admitted. And I hope you're hearing that I am not arguing very strongly for it, but I do think that it comes close to fitting the requirements for a dying declaration. And in the interests of justice, probably should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever read Judge Patricia Wald's article on this kind of evidence by any chance, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there has been a ruling from a Trial Chamber on the reading of statements of dead witnesses. It's one of the reasons I didn't make the application in respect of someone else. Mr. Ackerman candidly admits it doesn't fulfil the requirements of a dying declaration. At no stage were we notified that there was going to be any application to try and enter such a statement into evidence. It was held back until the time he had died. It's of -- Your Honour, apart from that, in any event, it's clearly untrue. Nonetheless, as a matter of principle, as I say, we object. Your Honour, and I think you've heard the...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, clearly untrue is the Prosecutor's submission, Your Honour, and nothing more. The decision that she refers to, she tells you there has been a decision of this Court on the matter. That's not true. There hasn't been a decision of this Tribunal on the matter. That decision had to do with someone who gave testimony at this Tribunal and later died, not someone who gave a statement with the knowledge their death was imminent. And so that doesn't even get close. This one at least gets close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll decide on this later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies. Next document, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the final group, it's 361 to 373, these are effectively part of the NIWD report that was attempted to be put in through Shoup. Your Honour, first of all, DB364, 365, 367, 368, 370, I think that must be, and 372 were not shown to Shoup at all. They are concerned with, many of them, what happened in Srebrenica, one of them, you'll remember, when I was raising an objection to them is Srebrenica under Tito. Your Honour, it's the same objection, if it is being tendered for the truth of what is in these articles, then, Your Honour, the proper way of getting them into evidence, was to call the writer, and not call Shoup and try and get them in through him. As I say, in any event, as far as 364, 365, 367-8, 370, and 372, they've never been shown to anyone, and we say they're inadmissable on that grounds. On the others, we say it's the evidence of Shoup that counts, if this is to be put in, again, for the truth of what's asserted, this is a -- it's not a memoir. It's a part of a book. Then, Your Honour, the writer should be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, there are two points to answer. One is the allegation or statement made by Ms. Korner that 374, 375, 377, 378, 370, 372 were never put to your expert witness in the course of his testimony. And secondly, then the other issue, 361 to 373, if you are tendering these documents as proof of their content without bringing the author, making him available to be cross-examination, Ms. Korner is objecting. So what's your position on the first and the second of these points?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I have, consequently, two points to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first is this: Your Honour will recall that one of the first things I did when I started talking to Dr. Shoup about these documents from NIWD was ask him his opinion of the work that was done by NIWD and whether he felt that it was responsible and proper and reliable and all of that. And he said that it was, based on his experience, and it was material that was professionally done and could be relied upon. So it is a secondary source upon which he placed some great reliance for the things he told you and he talked about those secondary sources. It has not been a rule yet in this trial that a document becomes inadmissible because it's not shown to a witness. You'll also recall that during the direct testimony of Professor Shoup, at one point, and I don't have the exact quote from the transcript, but at one point I said "Your Honours, in the interests of saving time, I am not going to show every one of these documents to Mr. Shoup and read part of it to him and ask him to agree that that's what it says because that would simply be wasting time. They are all sections of the NIWD report that he relied upon in arriving at his conclusions. So I think they are extraordinarily helpful to this Chamber in looking at his conclusions and seeing if it's supported by the documents that were tendered as exhibits to support it." And if you find that those documents do support his testimony, I think that adds weight to his testimony. But that's what they are. That's what they are here for. And I think they are entirely and completely admissible for that point. We're back to the position where you get to decide at the end of this case how much weight you give a document, whether you give it any weight at all. But to say that it's not admissible because it was not shown to a witness is just not, I don't think, a proper ruling. You'd have to throw out hundreds of the Prosecution's exhibits on that basis because many of their exhibits were never shown to a witness. Some were just read to you by Ms. Korner in Court without being shown to a witness. And I don't think that gives them any more admissibility just because she reads them to you. And I think that's what I have to say about them. I think they're absolutely admissible. I understand that they hurt Ms. Korner's case, and she would prefer that they are not here. But that's also not a reason for keeping them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I I'll leave that particular red rag aside. Your Honour, the difference is this: What you're getting here is not original documents. None of the documents that are even relied upon are available to us. What you're getting is somebody's ideas on an area that has nothing to do with this case at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ultimately -- sorry to interrupt you like this. But ultimately, if you're correct, and probably you are very correct in this submission, what's the end result? The bottom line is what? If they remain in the records?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the -- Your Honour, I personally don't mind at all. I think it's important that we follow the Rules of Evidence such as they are. And this is not in the category of an original document which can be looked at and about which evidence can be called. We can't see the original documents. We're looking at a writer -- I don't even know who this one is, in fact. But how can Srebrenica in Tito's time -- it has to be some relevance to the case, rather than, just, I want to throw everything in. But Mr. Ackerman obviously wants to rely on what I'm not sure. And if I don't object to them, Your Honours can rule them in, but effectively then the hands of the Court are tied in other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just to very quickly respond, I don't have it with me, but there is a section of Mr. Donia's report where he has talked at length about what was going on in Slovenia and Croatia and Serbia and other places in 1899, 1999, 1990, 1991. He says that the Court cannot understand what happened in Bosnia without understanding what happened in these other republics. And I also submit you can't understand what happened in the Krajina without understanding what happened in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it's very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you expect us to be satisfied in addition with just reading those documents and say "this is true," because Professor Shoup believes that the report of NIWD is completely reliable, so take his word, and that's it? This is proof of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you treat it the same way as you treat Dr. Donia's report and other things like that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're professional Judges, so you treat it the way you decide to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the message I tried to send when I addressed Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's at page 31 of Dr. Donia's report where he does that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One other thing, Ms. Korner, I may be completely wrong, and I apologise to you if I am wrong, but I also have a recollection that at some point in time you had also objected to DB358. If you could check that. Maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll check that. Unfortunately, perhaps if -- 358, Your Honour, was the video that was played to Professor Shoup. "The Avoidable War." No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't. Your Honour, can I just mention this. I have been sent a message saying that a situation of not a defendant, an accused, of a witness being in imminent death was actually dealt with in another case, the Halilovic case, Your Honour, where a presiding officer was appointed to be present when the statement was taken. And that's what I mean. Even if none of the safeguards for these types of statements were being followed in that case, but it would have been possible. And that's part of my objection, had the Defence desired to get this in, to the Court to appoint an a presiding officer and given us to ask questions as well. But Your Honour, those are the only Defence exhibits I take objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When we're finished with that, I have a couple of other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are finished with that. Before you get to the other matters, Madam Registrar, can you report back to me about availability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the floor, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. Sorry for the interruption. We're trying to find a pseudonym and we were not able to find it. There was a witness -- let's just go into private session very briefly just to be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, having tendered all of the Defence exhibits except for those which I have agreed to withdraw, having made every objection I could think of, the Defence rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you are correct that 259 -- wait a minute. You say 259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have several actually. 259. Perhaps you can come back to us tomorrow. 259, 260, 253 and 254 and 256 and 259. 259 we covered it already. And then 290.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: None of those are on my list of withdrawn exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 277 and 278. Again, I want to verify and make sure whether these are still in the records or whether they have been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They have not been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I tell you 290, 277 and 278 because there is also a Prosecution corresponding number for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think that's a problem, to have a corresponding number. They have got two Prosecution numbers for many exhibits. I just don't think that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could check on what I told you, please, and come back to us tomorrow morning just in case the information that I have is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've not withdrawn any of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Thank you. All right. Shall we reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. I am not in a position to tell you which courtroom, but I'm sure you will check, and we should finish tomorrow then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
